result: E2 treatment increases the expression of T-type calcium channels (Cacna1g) and HCN channels (Hcn1, Hcn2) in Kiss1ARH neurons, leading to increased T-type calcium and h-currents, and enhanced neuronal excitability measured as rebound excitation.
evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C30-C32, C35-C37 are well-supported by qPCR data (Figure 2A) showing significant increases in Cacna1g, Hcn1, and Hcn2 mRNA expression, and electrophysiological measurements (Figure 2B,C) demonstrating increased current densities and rebound excitation in E2-treated animals. Statistical significance is reported with appropriate p-values.

result: E2 treatment decreases the mRNA expression of neuropeptides Kiss1, Tac2 (NKB), Pdyn (dynorphin), and Tacr3 in Kiss1ARH neurons.
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C33, C34, C40, C41 are supported by qPCR data (Figures 2A, 3) showing significant reductions in Kiss1, Tac2, Pdyn, and Tacr3 mRNA levels in E2-treated versus oil-treated OVX females. This is consistent with established knowledge cited from prior literature and confirmed experimentally.

result: E2 treatment increases Slc17a6 (vGluT2) mRNA expression approximately 2-fold in Kiss1ARH neurons, indicating differential regulation of glutamate versus neuropeptide neurotransmitters by E2 in females.
evaluation: Claims C5, C38, C42 are supported by qPCR data (Figure 3) showing approximately 2-fold higher Slc17a6 mRNA levels in E2-treated versus oil-treated OVX females. The inference that glutamate is regulated differently than neuropeptides is reasonable given the opposing directional changes.

result: E2 treatment increases glutamatergic synaptic input to POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons from Kiss1ARH neurons, as evidenced by significantly lower paired-pulse ratios indicating greater probability of glutamate release.
evaluation: Claims C6, C50-C52 are supported by paired-pulse ratio experiments (Figure 5) showing significantly lower PPR in E2-treated versus oil-treated animals in both POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons. The interpretation that lower PPR indicates greater release probability is based on established synaptic physiology principles.

result: Optogenetic stimulation of Kiss1ARH neurons evokes glutamatergic responses in POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons that are blocked by AMPA/NMDA receptor antagonists and rescued by 4-AP after TTX blockade, providing biophysical evidence for direct synaptic signaling.
evaluation: Claims C43-C47 are supported by optogenetic electrophysiology data (Figure 4) showing light-evoked inward currents blocked by CNQX/AP5 and rescued by 4-AP in the presence of TTX. The TTX+4-AP rescue is established biophysical evidence for monosynaptic connections, properly cited.

result: High-frequency (20 Hz) optogenetic stimulation of Kiss1ARH neurons excites POMC neurons via metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluR1/5), generating slow EPSCs and depolarization that increases firing rate.
evaluation: Claims C7, C60, C61, C67, C69-C72 are supported by optogenetic data (Figure 7) showing slow EPSCs and depolarization in POMC neurons, scRT-PCR data (Figure 8) showing mGluR1/5 expression, and pharmacology (Figure 9) showing DHPG-induced depolarization. The reversal potential at -30 mV is consistent with cationic current activation.

result: High-frequency optogenetic stimulation of Kiss1ARH neurons inhibits NPY/AgRP neurons via metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluR2/7), generating slow IPSCs and hyperpolarization through GIRK channel activation, with enhanced responses in E2-treated animals.
evaluation: Claims C8, C62-C64, C68, C74-C77, C79-C81, C83-C84 are supported by optogenetic data (Figure 7) showing slow IPSCs, scRT-PCR (Figure 8) showing mGluR2/7 expression, pharmacology (Figure 10) showing DCG-IV and AMN082-induced hyperpolarization with reversal at EK+, and qPCR showing increased mGluR7 expression with E2. The mGluR7 antagonist ADX71743 blocked ~90% of the response.

result: Kiss1ARH neurons send direct glutamatergic projections to Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons, with enhanced glutamatergic input in E2-treated females as evidenced by reduced paired-pulse ratios.
evaluation: Claims C54-C59 are supported by immunocytochemistry (Figure 6A) showing ChR2-mCherry labeled fibers in AVPV/PeN without cell bodies, optogenetic data (Figure 6C) showing TTX-sensitive, 4-AP-rescued responses, and PPR experiments (Figure 6D,E) showing reduced PPR in E2-treated animals.

result: Conditional deletion of Slc17a6 in Kiss1 neurons eliminates fast glutamatergic responses in Kiss1AVPV/PeN, POMC, and NPY/AgRP neurons following low-frequency optogenetic stimulation.
evaluation: Claims C9, C85, C89-C91, C126 are supported by scRT-PCR (Figure 11A) confirming absence of Slc17a6 mRNA in KO neurons while Tac2 is present, and optogenetic experiments (Figure 12) showing complete absence of fast glutamatergic responses in all three target neuron populations from KO animals.

result: Deletion of Slc17a6 in Kiss1 neurons leads to conditioned place preference for sucrose and increased sucrose consumption in E2-treated KO female mice, with Het mice showing intermediate phenotype, while control E2-treated females show diminished motivation for sucrose.
evaluation: Claims C10, C107-C114, C127 are supported by CPP behavioral data (Figure 16A,B) showing significant preference for sucrose-paired chamber and increased sucrose intake in KO mice, with Het mice showing intermediate effects. Statistical analyses with appropriate two-way ANOVA and post-hoc tests are reported. The gene-dosage effect is supported by qPCR showing ~35% Slc17a6 expression in Het mice.

result: High-frequency stimulation of Kiss1ARH neurons in Slc17a6 KO mice evokes small residual currents in POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons, likely mediated by kisspeptin acting through Kiss1 receptors (GPR54) in POMC neurons and NPFFR1 in NPY/AgRP neurons.
evaluation: Claims C92-C94, C95-C96, C100-C105 are supported by optogenetic data (Figure 12H-J) showing small residual currents in KO animals, scRT-PCR (Figures 13D, 14A) showing receptor expression, and pharmacology (Figures 13, 14) showing kisspeptin and RFRP-3 effects. However, C94 is speculative as selective peptide antagonists were not available to definitively prove kisspeptin mediation.

result: Deletion of Slc17a6 in Kiss1 neurons significantly reduces the slow EPSP amplitude in Kiss1ARH neurons from E2-treated but not oil-treated OVX females, suggesting glutamate contributes to the slow EPSP in E2-treated animals.
evaluation: Claims C86-C88 are supported by optogenetic data (Figure 11) showing similar slow EPSP amplitudes in oil-treated control and KO mice, but significantly reduced slow EPSP in E2-treated KO versus control mice. The inference that glutamate contributes to the slow EPSP in E2-treated animals is reasonable given the data.

result: Deletion of Slc17a6 in Kiss1 neurons does not affect estrous cycle length or time to conception in female mice.
evaluation: Claims C119-C120 are supported by estrous cycle monitoring and fertility measurements showing no significant differences between WT, Het, and KO groups (one-way ANOVA, p=0.68 for both measures). However, the authors note that cycle staging was not confirmed by hormone measurements, which is a limitation.

result: Tac2 mRNA is the most highly expressed transcript in Kiss1ARH neurons from OVX females, with expression levels 50-fold higher than Pdyn/Kiss1 and 6-fold higher than Slc17a6 in OVX females, and 18-fold higher than Pdyn in E2-treated females.
evaluation: Claims C27-C29 are supported by qPCR data (Figure 1) with quantitative analysis using Tacr3 as calibrator. The fold-change calculations are based on CT values and appear methodologically sound. This establishes the relative abundance of different transcripts in Kiss1ARH neurons.

result: Slc32a1 (vGAT) mRNA was undetectable in Kiss1ARH neurons from both oil-treated and E2-treated OVX female mice.
evaluation: Claim C39 is supported by qPCR data showing Slc32a1 mRNA below the level of detectability (CT 36) in Kiss1ARH neurons. This indicates that GABA is not a primary neurotransmitter in these neurons, consistent with the functional data showing glutamate as the primary amino acid neurotransmitter.

result: Low-frequency optogenetic stimulation of Kiss1ARH neurons produces equivalent fast glutamatergic input to both POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons in females, similar to findings in males.
evaluation: Claims C48-C49 are supported by electrophysiological measurements showing no significant difference in evoked fast PSC amplitudes between POMC (25.8 ± 4.8 pA) and NPY/AgRP (33.3 ± 4.9 pA) neurons. The comparison to males is appropriately cited (Nestor et al., 2016).

result: There is a striking male/female difference in the effects of sex steroids on Slc17a6 mRNA expression and glutamate release in Kiss1ARH neurons, with testosterone inhibiting and estradiol enhancing glutamate signaling.
evaluation: Claim C53 is supported by the current findings showing E2 increases Slc17a6 expression and glutamate release in females, contrasted with cited findings (Nestor et al., 2016) showing testosterone decreases these parameters in males. This represents an important sex difference in neuroendocrine regulation.

result: Slc17a6 KO and Het mice did not show significant weight gain on standard chow over the study period, though Het mice showed statistically significant weight gain compared to controls. Slc17a6 mRNA in Het mice was ~35% of controls, and was undetectable in KO mice.
evaluation: Claims C106, C115-C117 are supported by body weight measurements (Figure 16C) and qPCR data (Figure 16D). The lack of significant weight gain in KO mice on standard chow, despite increased motivation for palatable food, suggests the phenotype is specific to hedonic rather than homeostatic feeding.

result: Intact males, which have reduced Slc17a6 mRNA expression and glutamate release compared to E2-treated females, demonstrated motivation for sucrose based on CPP.
evaluation: Claim C118 is supported by behavioral data (Figure 16—figure supplement 1) showing intact males developed CPP for sucrose, and is consistent with cited findings (Nestor et al., 2016) showing reduced Slc17a6 expression in intact versus castrated males. This provides additional context for the sex-specific regulation.

result: The E2-driven increase in Kiss1 neuronal excitability and glutamate neurotransmission may play a key role in governing motivational drive for palatable food and coordinating feeding and reproduction in females.
evaluation: Claims C11 and C128 are speculative conclusions that integrate multiple findings. While the data support that glutamate from Kiss1ARH neurons influences motivation for palatable food, the precise mechanisms and the coordination with reproduction require additional experiments. The claims appropriately use cautious language ('may play a key role').

result: Background claims about Kiss1 neuron populations, their regulation by E2, expression of neurotransmitters and receptors, and their roles in reproduction and feeding, based on cited literature.
evaluation: Claims C12-C26, C97-C98, C121-C122 are background knowledge claims supported by appropriate citations to published literature. These establish the context for the current study and are generally well-established in the field. The citations appear appropriate and accurate.

result: High-frequency stimulation of Kiss1ARH neurons produces significantly different membrane potential changes in POMC versus NPY/AgRP neurons, with excitation of POMC and inhibition of NPY/AgRP neurons, presumably through glutamate spillover to extrasynaptic metabotropic receptors.
evaluation: Claims C65-C66 are supported by electrophysiological data (Figure 7F) showing statistically significant differences in membrane potential changes. The mechanism involving glutamate spillover is appropriately cited (Nietz et al., 2017; Watanabe and Nakanishi, 2003) and is consistent with the high-frequency stimulation paradigm.

result: DHPG had no effect on NPY/AgRP neurons, DCG-IV had no effect on POMC neurons, and AMN082 had no effect on POMC neurons that responded to DHPG.
evaluation: Claims C73, C78, C82 are stated as negative results but the data are not shown. While these negative controls are important for establishing receptor specificity, the lack of presented data makes it difficult to fully evaluate these claims. The results are consistent with the scRT-PCR data showing differential receptor expression.

result: Summary claims integrating findings that E2 differentially regulates amino acid versus peptide neurotransmitters in Kiss1ARH neurons, increases neuronal excitability, and enables frequency-dependent glutamatergic and peptidergic neurotransmission to feeding-related neurons.
evaluation: Claims C123-C125 are summary statements that accurately integrate the experimental findings presented in the manuscript. These conclusions are well-supported by the collective data from molecular, electrophysiological, and behavioral experiments.
